newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Dutch see EU border pact with Norway, not Britain.
newsitem.headline: Dutch see EU border pact with Norway, not Britain.

text.p: Britain and Ireland would be left out of decision-making in a future border-free European Union while non-EU members could be allowed an active role, the Dutch EU presidency suggested on Monday.

Under a proposal put to EU treaty negotiators, officials from Norway and Iceland could find themselves sitting in EU buildings voting on matters concerning the border-free Schengen area, while representatives from London and Dublin sat silent.

"These countries are Schengen members," a Dutch diplomat said, referring to the two non-EU countries. "It would be difficult to imagine that Schengen members could not sit in on decision-making procedures."
At issue is the future of the 1985 Schengen Agreement, a pact between mostly EU countries under which border controls have been dropped and cooperation on police matters enhanced.
A number of EU member states have been pushing for the agreement to be brought into the EU proper when a new treaty for the 15-nation bloc is agreed, possibly this summer.
One problem has been that not all EU countries have signed up for Schengen, while another has been that some non-EU members have now joined.
Sovereignty- and security-conscious Britain says it has no intention of lifting its border controls. Ireland, which has an open border with Britain, cannot join Schengen without London.

Germany, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, Luxembourg, Spain and Portugal are full Schengen members. Austria, Italy, Greece, Denmark, Finland and Sweden have signed but not yet fully implemented the pact.
Norway and Iceland, which share a passport-free union with the EU's Nordic countries, have cooperation agreements.
Under one Dutch proposal, a copy of which was obtained by Reuters, the Schengen Agreement would be attached to the EU treaty as a protocol.
It suggests that administration of the pact could be carried out by EU officials in the Council of Ministers with jurisdiction for disputes handed to the European Court of Justice.

"The UK and Ireland would sit in the Council, but would take no part in its deliberations," the proposal says. "A provision could be included...to allow the participation of representatives of Iceland and Norway."
Norway has twice rejected EU membership. Iceland has said it does not wish to join.
The proposal makes much use of the term "flexibility", currently a buzz word in EU circles for allowing some countries to integrate faster than others.
Some countries have worried publicly that flexibility could damage the EU by fragmenting it, a concern that could be highlighted by the Dutch Schengen proposal.
